# 1. Overview

This notebook walks through a **complete supervised classification pipeline**
in R using two classic algorithms — **Decision Trees** and **k-Nearest
Neighbors (KNN)** — applied to R's built-in `iris` dataset. Using a built-in
dataset means the notebook runs end-to-end with no external files, which
makes it a convenient template you can later re-point at your own data.

The pipeline has 9 stages:

1. **Load & explore data** — inspect structure, summary statistics, and class balance.
2. **Visualize relationships** — pairwise scatterplots and boxplots by class.
3. **Preprocess** — check for missing values and split into train/test sets.
4. **Decision Tree — model building** — fit a classification tree with `rpart`.
5. **Decision Tree — visualization & pruning** — plot the tree and control overfitting via the complexity parameter.
6. **Decision Tree — evaluation** — confusion matrix, accuracy, precision/recall, variable importance.
7. **KNN — preprocessing & model building** — scale features (required for KNN) and fit models across a range of *k*.
8. **KNN — evaluation** — confusion matrix, accuracy, and an accuracy-vs-*k* curve to select the best *k*.
9. **Model comparison & save outputs** — compare both models side by side and export results.

> **Why this matters:** Decision Trees and KNN sit at opposite ends of the
> "how does the model think" spectrum. A tree learns explicit, human-readable
> **if–then rules** and is invariant to feature scaling. KNN makes no explicit
> model at all — it classifies a new point by majority vote among its
> nearest neighbors in feature space — and is *highly* sensitive to feature
> scaling and to the choice of *k*. Comparing them side by side on the same
> data is one of the best ways to build intuition for the bias–variance
> trade-off and for how an algorithm's assumptions shape its decision
> boundary.

---

# 2. Packages

We rely on several packages, each handling a different part of the pipeline:

| Package | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `tidyverse` | Core data wrangling and plotting (`dplyr`, `ggplot2`, `tidyr`, etc.) |
| `caret` | Train/test partitioning, confusion matrix utilities, cross-validation, unified model training |
| `rpart` | Fits classification/regression trees (CART algorithm) |
| `rpart.plot` | Produces readable, publication-quality decision tree diagrams |
| `class` | Implements the `knn()` classifier |
| `GGally` | `ggpairs()` for a matrix of pairwise scatterplots colored by class |
| `e1071` | Backend statistical utilities required internally by `caret` |

```{r packages}
# List of required packages
packages <- c("tidyverse", "caret", "rpart", "rpart.plot",
              "class", "GGally", "e1071")

# Check which packages are already installed on this machine
installed_packages <- rownames(installed.packages())

for (pkg in packages) {
  # Install only if missing
  if (!(pkg %in% installed_packages)) {
    install.packages(pkg, dependencies = TRUE)
  }
  # Load the package into the current session
  library(pkg, character.only = TRUE)
}

# Fix the random seed everywhere in this notebook so that the train/test
# split, tree fitting (which has some randomness in tie-breaking), and KNN
# results are exactly reproducible on re-run.
set.seed(42)
```

# 3. The Dataset: `iris`

`iris` is one of R's built-in datasets (no download needed — just type
`data(iris)`). It contains 150 flowers from 3 species of *Iris*
(*setosa*, *versicolor*, *virginica*), 50 each, with 4 numeric measurements
per flower. It is a standard benchmark for classification because it is
small, clean, and has one species (*setosa*) that is linearly separable and
two (*versicolor*, *virginica*) that overlap — giving both "easy" and
"hard" cases to evaluate a classifier on.

```{r load-data}
data(iris)

# ---- Basic structure ----
str(iris)

# ---- Summary statistics per numeric column ----
summary(iris)

# ---- Class balance: is this a balanced classification problem? ----
table(iris$Species)
```

**Variables:**

| Column | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `Sepal.Length` | numeric (cm) | Length of the sepal |
| `Sepal.Width` | numeric (cm) | Width of the sepal |
| `Petal.Length` | numeric (cm) | Length of the petal |
| `Petal.Width` | numeric (cm) | Width of the petal |
| `Species` | factor (3 levels) | **Target variable** — setosa / versicolor / virginica |

```{r check-missing}
# Always check for missing values before modeling — neither rpart nor knn()
# handles NAs gracefully by default.
cat("Total missing values:", sum(is.na(iris)), "\n")
```

---

# 4. Exploratory Visualization

Before modeling, it helps to *see* how separable the classes are in feature
space. This tells us, informally, what to expect from the classifiers below.

```{r pairs-plot, fig.width=8, fig.height=7}
# ggpairs() draws every pairwise combination of the 4 numeric features,
# colored by Species, plus per-feature density plots on the diagonal.
GGally::ggpairs(
  iris,
  columns = 1:4,
  aes(color = Species, alpha = 0.6)
) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r boxplots, fig.width=8, fig.height=5}
# Reshape to long format so all 4 features can be faceted in one ggplot call
iris_long <- iris %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -Species, names_to = "Feature", values_to = "Value")

ggplot(iris_long, aes(x = Species, y = Value, fill = Species)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, outlier.alpha = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ Feature, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Each Feature by Species",
       x = NULL, y = "Measurement (cm)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

> **What to notice:** `Petal.Length` and `Petal.Width` separate the three
> species almost perfectly, while `Sepal.Length` and `Sepal.Width` overlap
> considerably. This matters later — it explains why both models will lean
> heavily on the petal measurements, and it previews why *setosa* is easy to
> classify while *versicolor* vs. *virginica* is where most errors happen.

---

# 5. Preprocessing: Train/Test Split

We hold out part of the data to **evaluate generalization** — i.e., how well
the model performs on flowers it has never seen, not just the ones it was
fit on.

```{r train-test-split}
# createDataPartition() performs STRATIFIED sampling: it preserves the
# original class proportions in both the train and test sets, which is
# important here since a naive random split could (by chance) under- or
# over-represent a species in the test set.
train_index <- createDataPartition(iris$Species, p = 0.70, list = FALSE)

train_data <- iris[train_index, ]
test_data  <- iris[-train_index, ]

cat("Training rows:", nrow(train_data), "\n")
cat("Testing rows: ", nrow(test_data), "\n")

# Confirm the class balance was preserved in both sets
cat("\nTraining set class balance:\n")
print(table(train_data$Species))
cat("\nTest set class balance:\n")
print(table(test_data$Species))
```

> **Note on scaling:** Decision trees split on one feature at a time using
> threshold rules (e.g., `Petal.Length < 2.45`), so the *scale* of a feature
> does not affect the tree's structure — no scaling is needed for Section 6.
> KNN, by contrast, computes **Euclidean distance across all features
> simultaneously**, so a feature measured in larger units (or with larger
> variance) would dominate the distance calculation unless every feature is
> put on a common scale first. We scale the data specifically for the KNN
> section (Section 8) — see the note there for why we scale *after* rather
> than *before* the split.

---

# 6. Decision Tree — Model Building

A **classification tree** recursively splits the data on the feature and
threshold that most reduces class impurity (by default, the **Gini index**
in `rpart`), producing a set of nested if–then rules.

```{r fit-tree}
# method = "class" tells rpart this is a classification (not regression) tree.
# By default rpart() already applies a form of pre-pruning via its `cp`
# (complexity parameter) — see Section 7 for tuning this explicitly.
tree_model <- rpart(
  Species ~ Sepal.Length + Sepal.Width + Petal.Length + Petal.Width,
  data = train_data,
  method = "class"
)

# A text summary of the fitted tree: each node shows the split rule,
# number of observations, misclassifications, and predicted class.
print(tree_model)
```

## 6.1 Visualizing the Tree

```{r plot-tree, fig.width=7, fig.height=6}
# rpart.plot() gives a much more readable diagram than base plot(tree_model).
# extra = 104: show the predicted class, class probabilities, and the
# percentage of observations in each node.
rpart.plot(
  tree_model,
  type = 3, extra = 104, fallen.leaves = TRUE,
  main = "Classification Tree for Iris Species",
  box.palette = "auto"
)
```

## 6.2 Variable Importance

```{r tree-var-importance}
# rpart automatically computes an importance score for every predictor,
# even ones that never appear as a primary split (it credits "surrogate"
# splits too). Higher = more influential in the tree's decisions.
tree_model$variable.importance
```

---

# 7. Decision Tree — Pruning

A tree grown without any depth limit can **overfit**: it keeps splitting
until it perfectly memorizes the training data, which usually hurts
performance on new data. `rpart`'s complexity parameter `cp` controls this —
smaller `cp` allows more splits (more complex tree); larger `cp` forces a
simpler tree. `printcp()` reports the cross-validated error for a range of
`cp` values already tried during fitting.

```{r cp-table}
printcp(tree_model)
plotcp(tree_model)  # visualizes error vs. tree size; look for the "elbow"
```

```{r prune-tree}
# Standard rule of thumb: pick the cp with the lowest cross-validated
# error (xerror). which.min() finds that row automatically so this
# generalizes to any dataset without hand-reading the table above.
best_cp <- tree_model$cptable[which.min(tree_model$cptable[, "xerror"]), "CP"]
cat("Selected cp for pruning:", best_cp, "\n")

pruned_tree <- prune(tree_model, cp = best_cp)

rpart.plot(
  pruned_tree,
  type = 3, extra = 104, fallen.leaves = TRUE,
  main = "Pruned Classification Tree",
  box.palette = "auto"
)
```

> **On this dataset:** because `iris` is small and clean, the initial tree
> is often already at (or very near) its optimal size, so pruning may not
> change the tree at all. On noisier or larger datasets, this step
> typically removes several splits and is essential — always inspect
> `plotcp()` rather than skipping straight to prediction.

## 7.1 Predictions and Evaluation

```{r tree-predict}
tree_preds <- predict(pruned_tree, newdata = test_data, type = "class")

# confusionMatrix() (from caret) gives accuracy, per-class sensitivity/
# specificity, and other diagnostics in one call.
tree_cm <- confusionMatrix(tree_preds, test_data$Species)
tree_cm
```

```{r tree-cm-plot, fig.width=5, fig.height=4}
# A tidy heatmap version of the same confusion matrix is often easier to
# read at a glance than the console table above.
as.data.frame(tree_cm$table) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Reference, y = Prediction, fill = Freq)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = Freq), size = 5) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Decision Tree — Confusion Matrix", x = "Actual", y = "Predicted") +
  theme_minimal()
```

---

# 8. k-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)

KNN classifies a new observation by finding its *k* closest points (by
Euclidean distance) in the **training** data and taking a majority vote of
their labels. It has no separate "training" phase in the usual sense — all
the work happens at prediction time — which makes the choice of *k* and the
feature scale the two things that matter most.

## 8.1 Feature Scaling

```{r knn-scale}
# --------------------------------------------------------------------
# IMPORTANT: we compute the scaling parameters (mean, sd) from the
# TRAINING set only, then apply that SAME transformation to the test set.
# Scaling using statistics from the full dataset (train + test combined)
# would leak information about the test set into training — a common and
# subtle source of overly optimistic accuracy in KNN pipelines.
# --------------------------------------------------------------------
feature_cols <- c("Sepal.Length", "Sepal.Width", "Petal.Length", "Petal.Width")

preproc <- preProcess(train_data[, feature_cols], method = c("center", "scale"))

train_scaled <- predict(preproc, train_data[, feature_cols])
test_scaled  <- predict(preproc, test_data[, feature_cols])

# Labels are kept separately, since knn() takes them as their own argument
train_labels <- train_data$Species
test_labels  <- test_data$Species

summary(train_scaled)  # each feature should now have mean ~0, sd ~1
```

## 8.2 Choosing *k*

*k* is the central hyperparameter of KNN:

- **Small *k* (e.g., 1–3):** the model follows the training data very
  closely — low bias, high variance (sensitive to noise/outliers,
  prone to overfitting).
- **Large *k*:** predictions are smoothed over many neighbors — higher
  bias, lower variance (can underfit, and may blur genuine class
  boundaries).

We evaluate a range of *k* values on the test set and plot accuracy against
*k* to choose a good balance.

```{r knn-choose-k}
k_values <- 1:20

# For each candidate k, fit and evaluate a KNN model, storing accuracy
accuracy_by_k <- map_dbl(k_values, function(k) {
  pred <- knn(train = train_scaled, test = test_scaled,
              cl = train_labels, k = k)
  mean(pred == test_labels)
})

k_results <- tibble(k = k_values, accuracy = accuracy_by_k)
best_k <- k_results$k[which.max(k_results$accuracy)]

cat("Best k (by test accuracy):", best_k, "\n")
```

```{r knn-k-plot, fig.width=7, fig.height=4}
ggplot(k_results, aes(x = k, y = accuracy)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue") +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = best_k, linetype = "dashed", color = "firebrick") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = k_values) +
  labs(title = "KNN Accuracy vs. k",
       subtitle = paste("Best k =", best_k),
       x = "k (number of neighbors)", y = "Test Accuracy") +
  theme_minimal()
```

> **A methodological caveat:** selecting *k* by directly maximizing
> **test-set** accuracy (as above, for simplicity) risks a mild form of
> overfitting to the test set itself. For a research-grade evaluation,
> prefer choosing *k* via **cross-validation on the training set only**
> (e.g., `caret::train(..., method = "knn", trControl = trainControl(method
> = "cv", number = 10))`), then evaluate the single chosen model once, on
> the untouched test set. An example of this more rigorous approach is
> given in Section 8.4.

## 8.3 Final KNN Model and Evaluation

```{r knn-final}
knn_preds <- knn(train = train_scaled, test = test_scaled,
                  cl = train_labels, k = best_k)

knn_cm <- confusionMatrix(knn_preds, test_labels)
knn_cm
```

```{r knn-cm-plot, fig.width=5, fig.height=4}
as.data.frame(knn_cm$table) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Reference, y = Prediction, fill = Freq)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = Freq), size = 5) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "darkorange") +
  labs(title = paste0("KNN (k=", best_k, ") — Confusion Matrix"),
       x = "Actual", y = "Predicted") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## 8.4 (Recommended) Cross-Validated KNN via `caret`

This alternative workflow selects *k* using 10-fold cross-validation on the
**training set only**, avoiding the test-set-leakage caveat noted above. It
is the version to prefer when reporting results formally (e.g., in a paper
or lab report).

```{r knn-caret-cv}
ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

knn_cv_model <- train(
  Species ~ Sepal.Length + Sepal.Width + Petal.Length + Petal.Width,
  data = train_data,
  method = "knn",
  trControl = ctrl,
  preProcess = c("center", "scale"),   # scaling is applied inside each CV fold
  tuneGrid = expand.grid(k = 1:20)
)

knn_cv_model
plot(knn_cv_model)  # cross-validated accuracy vs. k

# Evaluate the cross-validation-selected model once, on the held-out test set
knn_cv_preds <- predict(knn_cv_model, newdata = test_data)
confusionMatrix(knn_cv_preds, test_data$Species)
```

---

# 9. Model Comparison

```{r comparison-table}
comparison <- tibble(
  Model = c("Decision Tree (pruned)", "KNN (test-tuned)", "KNN (cross-validated)"),
  Accuracy = c(
    tree_cm$overall["Accuracy"],
    knn_cm$overall["Accuracy"],
    confusionMatrix(knn_cv_preds, test_data$Species)$overall["Accuracy"]
  ),
  Kappa = c(
    tree_cm$overall["Kappa"],
    knn_cm$overall["Kappa"],
    confusionMatrix(knn_cv_preds, test_data$Species)$overall["Kappa"]
  )
)

comparison
```

| Aspect | Decision Tree | KNN |
|---|---|---|
| **How it decides** | Learns explicit if–then split rules | Majority vote among *k* nearest points |
| **Feature scaling required?** | No | **Yes** — critical |
| **Interpretability** | High — the tree itself is the explanation | Low — no explicit model to inspect |
| **Training cost** | Higher (builds the tree once) | ~None (lazy learner) |
| **Prediction cost** | Very low (traverse the tree) | Higher (distance to every training point) |
| **Sensitive to** | Overfitting if unpruned | Choice of *k*; irrelevant/unscaled features; class imbalance |
| **Decision boundary shape** | Axis-aligned rectangles | Arbitrarily shaped, locally adaptive |

> **On `iris` specifically:** both models typically achieve high accuracy
> (often 90–100% on the test set) because `Petal.Length`/`Petal.Width` are
> so strongly class-separating. Most of whatever errors remain occur between
> *versicolor* and *virginica* — the two species whose boxplots overlapped
> in Section 4 — for **both** models, since both are ultimately limited by
> the same underlying feature overlap, not by an algorithmic weakness of
> either one.

# 10. Save Outputs

```{r save-outputs}
# Predictions and confusion matrices, for reuse in a report or paper
write_csv(
  test_data %>%
    mutate(Tree_Prediction = tree_preds, KNN_Prediction = knn_preds),
  "iris_test_predictions.csv"
)

write_csv(comparison, "model_comparison.csv")
write_csv(k_results, "knn_accuracy_by_k.csv")

# Save key plots
ggsave("decision_tree_plot.png", plot = last_plot(), width = 7, height = 6, dpi = 300)
ggsave("knn_accuracy_vs_k.png",
       plot = ggplot(k_results, aes(x = k, y = accuracy)) +
         geom_line(color = "steelblue") + geom_point() + theme_minimal(),
       width = 7, height = 4, dpi = 300)

cat("Saved files: iris_test_predictions.csv, model_comparison.csv,",
    "knn_accuracy_by_k.csv, decision_tree_plot.png, knn_accuracy_vs_k.png\n")
```

---

# 11. Summary

In this notebook, you learned how to:

- Explore and visualize a labeled classification dataset (`iris`) to
  anticipate which features drive class separation.
- Perform a **stratified** train/test split to preserve class proportions.
- Fit, visualize, and interpret a **Decision Tree** classifier with `rpart`
  and `rpart.plot`.
- Control tree overfitting via the complexity parameter (`cp`) and
  cross-validated pruning.
- Correctly **scale features** for KNN using statistics from the training
  set only (avoiding test-set leakage).
- Select the hyperparameter *k* both by direct test evaluation and by the
  more rigorous cross-validation approach (`caret::train`).
- Evaluate both models with confusion matrices, accuracy, and Cohen's Kappa,
  and compare their trade-offs conceptually.

**Next steps to try on your own:**

- Re-run this notebook on another built-in dataset, e.g. `mlbench::Sonar`
  (binary classification, many correlated numeric features) or
  `MASS::biopsy` (medical diagnosis), to see how the two models' relative
  performance changes when classes overlap more or features are noisier.
- Extend Section 9 with **ROC/AUC** analysis (`pROC` package) — straightforward
  for binary classification, requires a one-vs-rest approach for the
  3-class case here.
- Compare both models against a third baseline, such as logistic regression
  (binary case) or `nnet::multinom` (multi-class), to place their accuracy
  in context.
- Investigate **feature selection**: refit the Decision Tree and KNN using
  only `Petal.Length` and `Petal.Width` (the two most separating features
  from Section 4) and see whether accuracy changes.
